prompt: You create a bucket in sa-east-1. Where are its objects kept?
hint: A region is a place, not a label.

choices.text: Wherever the provider has spare capacity that day
choices.why: That is the picture the section replaces. A resource is created in one region and sits there.

choices.text: In São Paulo, until you configure a copy elsewhere
choices.why: Right. The provider does not copy it to another region on its own; replication is something you set up and pay for.

choices.text: In every region, so users anywhere read it fast
choices.why: Copies in other regions exist only if you create them, and each one moves data across a border you chose.

choices.text: In the region of the account that owns it
choices.why: An account has no region. One account holds resources in many regions, each chosen per resource.

prompt: One t3.micro runs for a 30-day month of 720 hours. How many dollars more does it cost in sa-east-1 than in us-east-1, at the sheet's on-demand prices?
hint: 0.01680 against 0.01040 an hour.

prompt: Across the on-demand lines of the sheet, how does the São Paulo price compare with the Virginia price for the same instance?
hint: Divide two lines.

choices.text: The same, since an instance type is the same machine everywhere
choices.why: The machine is the same; the price is not. Every line of the block has two different numbers.

choices.text: Exactly 1.5 times, a fixed regional multiplier
choices.why: There is no fixed multiplier: the ratios differ from line to line, from 1.54 to 1.62.

choices.text: Between 1.54 and 1.62 times, depending on the line
choices.why: Right. 0.01680 / 0.01040 is 1.615 and 0.13755 / 0.08925 is 1.541; the ratio moves a little from line to line.

choices.text: Lower, since the Brazilian region is newer
choices.why: Every line on the sheet is higher in sa-east-1. The sheet says what the prices are, not why.

prompt: Your design depends on a managed queue service the provider announced last month. Before anyone draws the architecture, what should you check?
hint: A region is not a copy of every other region.

choices.text: Its price in us-east-1, since new services are priced there first
choices.why: Price is a trade-off among regions that are still in the running; it does not tell you whether the service exists where you will run.

choices.text: Nothing: a service the provider announced exists in all its regions
choices.why: New services arrive in some regions before others, and some are missing from a region for years.

choices.text: The latency from your users to the provider's nearest edge location
choices.why: The edge caches and runs small code; a managed queue lives in a region, so the edge answers a different question.

choices.text: Whether the service exists in the region you must run in
choices.why: Right. If it does not, the choice is between redesigning without it and moving region, and the law might rule out the second.

prompt: What is an availability zone?
hint: AWS's own definition, in the section.

choices.text: One or more datacentres with their own power and network
choices.why: Right. Each zone is isolated from the others so that a building's failure stays in that zone.

choices.text: A single rack of servers, sharing one room's power and cooling
choices.why: A zone is at least a whole datacentre, and often several; a rack shares that room's power and cooling.

choices.text: Another name for a region
choices.why: A region holds several zones. The region is chosen for law, latency and price; zones are what you spread across.

choices.text: A city where the provider caches content near users
choices.why: That describes an edge location, which is neither a zone nor a region.

prompt: Your application runs in one AWS account and the database in another. Both teams placed their part "in sa-east-1a" to keep traffic inside one zone. What should they compare to be sure?
hint: A name is a label per account.

choices.text: The zone names, since both say sa-east-1a
choices.why: That is the trap: AWS maps names to physical zones independently per account, so matching names prove nothing.

choices.text: The zone IDs, such as sae1-az1
choices.why: Right. The zone ID names the same physical zone in every account.

choices.text: The region codes of the two accounts
choices.why: Both resources are in sa-east-1 already; the question is which building inside it, and a region code cannot answer that.

choices.text: The IP ranges each account received from ip-ranges.json
choices.why: That file lists AWS's public address blocks by region and service, not the mapping of your zone names.

prompt: A release with a bug is deployed to the instances in both zones at once, and the application starts failing. What did running in two zones do for you?
hint: Ask what kind of failure a zone is built to contain.

choices.text: It kept one zone healthy, because zones are isolated
choices.why: Zones isolate power, cooling and network. They do not isolate your own change when you push it to both.

choices.text: It rolled back the release in the second zone
choices.why: Nothing in a zone knows about your releases. A rollback is something your deployment process does.

choices.text: Nothing: the failure is not local to a building
choices.why: Right. Two zones defend against the ground under one building, and a bug shipped everywhere is not that.

choices.text: It moved traffic to another region automatically
choices.why: Zones are inside one region; moving to another region is a disaster recovery plan somebody has to build.

prompt: Two zones are 60 km apart in a straight line. At 200 km per millisecond in fibre, what is the minimum round-trip time between them, in milliseconds?
hint: There and back.

prompt: What is ip-ranges.json published for?
hint: Who needs a list of addresses?

choices.text: To announce new regions to customers
choices.why: It reflects regions, and it even carries some the CLI does not know, but announcing is not its job.

choices.text: To list the addresses your own instances will receive
choices.why: Your instances get addresses when you create them; this file lists AWS's public blocks, not assignments to you.

choices.text: For firewall rules that allow or block AWS addresses
choices.why: Right. An allow-list for S3 in São Paulo, or for the CDN in front of your server, is built from it.

choices.text: For billing, to show where your traffic went
choices.why: Billing is per account and needs one; this file needs no account at all.

prompt: In ip-ranges.json, 492 IPv4 blocks carry region "GLOBAL", many of them CLOUDFRONT and GLOBALACCELERATOR. What does that value mean?
hint: Look at the services under it.

choices.text: A region in the United States that serves the whole world
choices.why: There is no such region. The label marks addresses that are not tied to any one region.

choices.text: Services that answer from many places at once
choices.why: Right. A CDN and a global entry point answer near the user, wherever that is.

choices.text: Blocks that are reserved and not yet used by any service
choices.why: The services named under it are in use; CloudFront alone has 118 of those blocks.

choices.text: A partition like China or GovCloud
choices.why: Those are separate partitions with their own region codes, cn- and us-gov-. GLOBAL is none of them.

prompt: China, AWS GovCloud and the European Sovereign Cloud are separate copies of AWS with their own accounts. The CLI's list calls each of them a ___.
hint: The file is named after them.

prompt: Counting regions from ip-ranges.json, which values should you drop to get the regions an ordinary account can use? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three kinds of value do not belong in the count.

choices.text: GLOBAL
choices.why: Right. It labels addresses that belong to no single region.

choices.text: cn-north-1
choices.why: Right. It is in the aws-cn partition, which an ordinary account cannot use.

choices.text: sa-east-1
choices.why: São Paulo is an ordinary region that both files agree on.

choices.text: sa-west-1
choices.why: Right. It has address space and is unknown to CLI 2.37.4; what it is, neither file says.

prompt: A server is 1,000 km away in a straight line. What is the minimum round-trip time over fibre, in milliseconds?
hint: 200 km per millisecond, there and back.

prompt: floor.py says São Paulo to Ashburn is at least 76.6 ms. Why would a real ping come back slower?
hint: The program measured a line on a sphere.

choices.text: Because light in fibre is slower than 200 km per millisecond on long cables
choices.why: The speed in glass is the same on a long cable as a short one; the distance and the stops along it are what grow.

choices.text: Because the program rounds the distance down
choices.why: It prints to a tenth of a millisecond; the gap to a real measurement is not rounding.

choices.text: It would not: 76.6 ms is what a real ping measures
choices.why: Nothing in the section was measured on a network. The program computed a floor, and real paths only add to it.

choices.text: Cables follow coasts and landing points, and routers queue packets
choices.why: Right. The real path is longer than the great circle, and every router and server on it adds time.

prompt: A contract requires every answer to reach users in São Paulo within 30 ms, round trip included. The cheapest region is about 4,000 km away. What does the floor tell you before any test?
hint: Work out the floor for 4,000 km.

choices.text: Ruled out: the light alone needs 40 ms to go there and back
choices.why: Right. 2 x 4,000 / 200 is 40 ms, over 30 with a perfect network and an instant server.

choices.text: It is fine if the region has a fast enough link
choices.why: Bandwidth does not move the floor. At 4,000 km the light alone needs 40 ms there and back.

choices.text: Nothing: only a measurement settles latency
choices.why: A measurement tells you how far above the floor you are. The floor already rules this design out.

choices.text: It meets the contract with 10 ms to spare
choices.why: That reads 4,000 km as a one-way 20 ms and forgets the way back.

prompt: A page makes 12 API calls to Ashburn, each waiting for the one before. Using the floor of 76.6 ms per round trip, what is the minimum time spent waiting, in milliseconds?
hint: Sequential calls add up.

prompt: The page with twenty sequential calls to Virginia is slow. Someone proposes a link ten times faster. What does it change?
hint: Each answer is 2 KB.

choices.text: It cuts the wait to a tenth, about 153 ms
choices.why: That treats the wait as transfer time. The wait is the round trip, and bandwidth does not shorten it.

choices.text: Almost nothing: about 3 ms out of more than 1,500
choices.why: Right. A 2 KB answer takes 0.16 ms at 100 Mbit/s and 0.016 ms at ten times that; twenty of them save 2.9 ms.

choices.text: It removes the TLS handshakes
choices.why: Handshakes are round trips too, and a wider link does not make a round trip shorter. Reusing connections removes them.

choices.text: It halves the wait, since the answers arrive twice as fast
choices.why: Neither the arithmetic nor the cause fits: the time is the light crossing the continent, not the bytes.

prompt: The same code opens a new HTTPS connection for each of 10 sequential calls to Ashburn: a TCP handshake, a TLS 1.3 handshake, then the request. At a floor of 76.6 ms per round trip, what is the minimum total, in milliseconds?
hint: Three round trips per call.

prompt: Match each fix to what it saves.
hint: Every working fix makes fewer trips or shorter ones.

pairs.right: The waiting between calls that do not depend on each other

pairs.left: A region closer to the users
pairs.right: Part of the length of every trip

right_distractors: The time the bytes take to arrive

prompt: Which of the five questions does the section treat as constraints, able to rule a region out whatever it costs? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of the five are not trade-offs.

choices.text: What it costs there
choices.why: Price is weighed against the others among regions that pass the constraints.

choices.text: Whether the law lets the data be there
choices.why: Right. A region that breaks a residency rule is out, and so is a replica there.

choices.text: Where your other systems are
choices.why: It is a trade-off: it pushes chatty parts together, and a system can be moved.

choices.text: Whether a service you cannot do without exists there
choices.why: Right. Without it the region is out, unless you redesign without that service.

prompt: The clinic's nightly report uses anonymised data and nobody waits for it. It reads the records database in sa-east-1 twenty thousand times a night. Where does the section lean for running it?
hint: The fifth question.

choices.text: us-east-1, because an m7i.large is cheaper there
choices.why: The instance is cheaper, but twenty thousand reads across a continent pay in round trips and in transfer out of São Paulo.

choices.text: Next to the data, in sa-east-1
choices.why: Right. A job that talks to the database that many times belongs beside it; the cheaper instance is eaten by the distance.

choices.text: At the edge, since nobody waits for it
choices.why: Edge locations run small code near users; a batch job reading a database belongs in the database's region.

choices.text: In a different region every night, to spread the cost
choices.why: Moving it around does not change the distance to the one database it reads.

prompt: A company in Lisbon builds an app for customers who are all in Brazil. No law restricts where the data sits, and every service it needs exists in both sa-east-1 and eu-west-1. Which question now decides between them?
hint: The team is not the user.

choices.text: Where the team works, since they deploy every day
choices.why: The team pays the distance a few times a day; the customers pay it on every page they load.

choices.text: Nothing is left to decide: both pass the constraints
choices.why: Passing the constraints is where the trade-offs start, and the first of them points clearly one way here.

choices.text: Where the users are: Brazil, so sa-east-1
choices.why: Right. With both constraints passed, latency to the customers weighs most, and every one of them is in Brazil.

choices.text: The price, since the company pays the bill in euros
choices.why: The currency of the bill is not a question on the list, and the price is weighed after latency for customers who wait on every page.

prompt: How many zones does a single instance live in?
hint: Where does it go when its zone has a bad day?

choices.text: All the zones of its region
choices.why: That is the comfortable assumption the section starts by removing. One instance sits in one zone.

choices.text: Two, since the provider keeps a standby copy
choices.why: A standby exists only if you build one, and then it is a second instance you pay for.

choices.text: Exactly one
choices.why: Right. Surviving a zone means running a second instance in a second zone.

choices.text: None: instances live in the region
choices.why: A region is a group of zones; the instance runs in one of them.

prompt: An instance in sa-east-1b reads 800 GB a month from a database primary in sa-east-1a. The sheet charges 0.0100 per GB between zones, each direction. How many dollars a month does that traffic cost?
hint: Out of one zone, into the other.

prompt: Your application runs in two zones of sa-east-1, with a standby database, all correctly configured. A problem hits the provider's regional control systems for sa-east-1. What does the multi-AZ design protect you from?
hint: What do the two zones share?

choices.text: Nothing: a failure at the level of the region reaches both zones alike
choices.why: Right. Two zones survive a zone; a problem at the level of the region reaches every zone in it.

choices.text: All of it, since the standby is in another zone
choices.why: The standby protects against the primary's zone failing, not against a failure the two zones share.

choices.text: All of it: the load balancer moves traffic to a healthy region
choices.why: The load balancer spreads traffic across zones inside its own region; it has no second region to send it to.

choices.text: Half of it, since one zone keeps running
choices.why: Both zones are under the same regional systems, so there is no half that is outside the problem.

prompt: The zone holding the database primary fails. Put the steps of the failover in order.
hint: The standby has to become something before anyone can use it.
items: The standby is promoted to primary
The application reconnects to the new primary
trap: Reconnecting before the promotion finds a standby that still refuses writes.

prompt: How much data you can afford to lose after a disaster, measured in time, is the ___.
hint: Three letters; the P is for point.

prompt: How long the business can afford the system to be down is the ___.
hint: Three letters; the T is for time.

prompt: Put the disaster recovery strategies in order of what they cost to keep, cheapest first.
hint: Count what is running in the second region.
trap: Pilot light before warm standby: its servers are defined and switched off, where warm standby keeps a small copy running.

prompt: A database in sa-east-1 replicates 200 GB a month to a standby in us-east-1. The sheet charges 0.1380 per GB from sa-east-1 to the other region. How many dollars a month is the transfer?
hint: The price of the region the data leaves.

prompt: The same 500 GB replicated from São Paulo to Virginia costs 69.00 dollars, and from Virginia to São Paulo 10.00. What sets the price?
hint: Read the two columns of one line.

choices.text: The region the data arrives in
choices.why: Data coming in is priced at 0.0000 on the sheet; the charge is on the way out.

choices.text: The distance between the regions
choices.why: The distance is the same in both directions, and the prices are not.

choices.text: Which region holds the primary database
choices.why: The primary matters only because the data leaves from it; a copy flowing the other way is priced by its own source.

choices.text: The region the data leaves
choices.why: Right. Each column is the price of data leaving that region: 0.1380 out of sa-east-1, 0.0200 out of us-east-1.

prompt: A team wants zero data loss between São Paulo and Virginia, and proposes synchronous replication. What does the floor predict for their database?
hint: A synchronous commit waits for the other copy.

choices.text: No change, since replication happens in the background
choices.why: That describes asynchronous replication, the kind that loses what was in flight. Synchronous means the commit waits.

choices.text: Every commit waits at least 76.6 ms for Virginia
choices.why: Right. Each commit pays the round trip before it is confirmed, which is why cross-region replication is mostly asynchronous.

choices.text: Commits wait about 1 ms, as between zones
choices.why: The 1 ms floor is for zones within 100 km. Virginia is 7,664 km away.

choices.text: Commits get faster, since two databases share the load
choices.why: A synchronous standby does not share the writes; it adds a wait to each one.

prompt: Match each strategy to what runs in the second region.
hint: From nothing running to everything serving.

pairs.right: Copies of the data and nothing running
Replicated data, servers defined and switched off
A small complete copy, taking no customer traffic
A full copy serving real users

right_distractors: A second zone in the same region

prompt: What does an edge location do well?
hint: Two things, per the section.

choices.text: Keeps copies of content and runs small code
choices.why: Right. Caching and small functions, a short trip from the user.

choices.text: Hosts your database close to users
choices.why: The system of record stays in a region, with zones and durable storage behind it.

choices.text: Offers every service of a region, in more places
choices.why: An edge location is a small site, often a rack; it does not carry a region's catalogue.

choices.text: Replaces availability zones for failover
choices.why: Zones are inside a region and hold your running systems; the edge is neither.

prompt: A function at an edge location in Fortaleza answers each request by querying a database in Virginia five times, one query after another. Compared with a server beside the database, the page is:
hint: Count the long trips.

choices.text: Faster, since the user reached the edge in a short trip
choices.why: The user saved one short trip, and the function then spent five long ones.

choices.text: The same, since the database does the same work
choices.why: The work is the same; the trips to reach it are not.

choices.text: Slower: five long trips replace five very short ones
choices.why: Right. Beside the database, those five queries cross almost no distance; from the edge, each one crosses a continent.

choices.text: Faster, if the edge caches the query results
choices.why: Results that are personal to the request are not the same for everybody, and a cache helps only what is.

prompt: Match each piece to where the section puts it.
hint: Copies and small code at the edge; the truth in the region.

pairs.right: An edge cache, copied near users

pairs.left: A check of a signed token
pairs.right: Code at the edge, near the user

pairs.left: A page that queries the database twenty times

right_distractors: A single zone, with no copy

prompt: Launching a new instance is a call to which part of the service?
hint: Creating, changing, deleting.

choices.text: The data plane
choices.why: The data plane runs what already exists: the instance answering, the bucket serving.

choices.text: The edge
choices.why: The edge caches and runs small code near users; it does not create instances.

choices.text: The load balancer itself
choices.why: A load balancer forwards traffic to instances that already exist, which is data-plane work.

choices.text: The control plane
choices.why: Right. Creating, changing and deleting go through the control plane.

prompt: Two designs survive the loss of zone a. Design one launches replacement instances in zone b when a fails. Design two already runs enough capacity in zone b. During a control-plane problem, which one still works?
hint: Which step needs the control plane?

choices.text: Design one, since launching is quicker than keeping idle capacity
choices.why: Launching is a control-plane call, and the control plane is the part that is failing.

choices.text: Design two: health checks are data-plane work
choices.why: Right. That is static stability: nothing has to change for it to keep working.

choices.text: Both, since each survives the loss of a zone
choices.why: Both survive a zone on a normal day. Only one survives it on a day the control plane is also in trouble.

choices.text: Neither, since a control-plane problem stops running instances
choices.why: Running instances are data plane and keep serving; what stops is creating and changing things.

prompt: Everything you run is in sa-east-1. Your failover plan starts with "point the DNS record at the standby". Which region's health does that first step depend on?
hint: Where do the control planes of some global services run?

choices.text: us-east-1, where DNS changes are made
choices.why: Right. AWS documents Route 53's control plane in us-east-1, a region you never chose.

choices.text: sa-east-1 only, since everything you run is there
choices.why: Your resources are there; the control plane that edits DNS records is not.

choices.text: None, since DNS is a global service
choices.why: Its data plane is spread out and keeps answering. Changing a record is a control-plane call, and that runs in one region.

choices.text: The region of the edge location nearest your users
choices.why: Edge locations answer queries and cache content; the change goes through the control plane, not the edge.

prompt: A system that keeps working through a failure without having to change anything has what AWS calls static ___.
hint: The property the section names.

prompt: A checkout page in São Paulo makes 6 sequential calls to an API in Frankfurt. Which single change removes the most waiting?
hint: Compare the floors: 98.3 ms per trip to Frankfurt.

choices.text: Moving the API to São Paulo
choices.why: Right. The six trips then cross a city instead of an ocean, which removes almost all of the 589.8 ms.

choices.text: A link with ten times the bandwidth
choices.why: Bandwidth leaves the 98.3 ms floor untouched; six trips still cost at least 589.8 ms.

choices.text: Moving the API to Virginia
choices.why: Six trips at 76.6 ms is 459.6 ms: shorter than Frankfurt, and still the long way.

choices.text: Caching the page at an edge location in São Paulo
choices.why: A checkout page is personal to the user; a cache helps only what is the same for everybody.

prompt: Match each number from this lesson to what it is.
hint: Two are prices per GB, one is a time.

pairs.right: Per GB between zones, each direction
Per GB out of sa-east-1 to the other region
Per GB out of us-east-1 to the other region
The floor from São Paulo to Ashburn and back

right_distractors: Per GB in from the internet

prompt: Put these round trips from a server in São Paulo in order of their floor, shortest first.
hint: One millisecond per 100 km of straight line.
trap: Ashburn before Frankfurt: 7,664 km against 9,829 km, so 76.6 ms against 98.3 ms.
